tour.title: “No sin worthy of death” in Deuteronomy 22:26
tour.intro: This short tour follows Deuteronomy 22:26 in its immediate setting: a betrothed woman is attacked in the open country, and the law explicitly refuses to treat her as guilty. You’ll hear the passage framed within Israel’s community laws, then hear the crucial comparison to murder, and finally get help with the ancient betrothal terminology behind the case.

steps.why: Start here for the larger legal frame. The hosts describe these chapters as Moses “unpacking the Ten Commandments” and explain that “don’t commit adultery” expands to include “laws about rape” and “deceitful” consensual relationships. That helps you hear Deuteronomy 22:26 as part of a concern for how people are treated in community, not as an isolated rule.

This is the clearest direct treatment of the verse. The teacher distinguishes the case of a woman who “cries out, but nobody can hear her,” says “she’s innocent,” and explains that verse 26 “equates rape with murder in a sense.” In other words, “no sin worthy of death” identifies the woman as not legally culpable; the death sentence falls on the attacker.

Finish by hearing the legal and cultural distinction underneath the passage. The speaker contrasts the city case with the open-country case, notes that the presumption is that the woman “cried out,” and says plainly, “That’s rape.” He also explains why the text calls the betrothed woman a “neighbor’s wife”: betrothal carried legal status like marriage in that setting.

tour.closing: Taken together, these clips make the sentence’s force clear: Deuteronomy 22:26 is not saying the assault is morally insignificant. It is saying that the woman has committed no capital offense and must not be punished as though she consented; the text compares the attacker’s violence to murder and assigns guilt to him.
